tabIntros.note: Analyst summaries generated by Claude from the prior day's snapshot. Each paragraph states the key finding for that tab with specific numbers and connects to related tabs.

intros.market: Five CAs control 88% of all publicly trusted certificate issuance, with Let's Encrypt (32%), Google Trust Services (21%), and DigiCert (18%) holding a combined 71% market share. The market HHI of 1984 indicates high concentration, near the threshold that triggers antitrust scrutiny in other industries. Despite 88 CAs holding trusted roots, 74 operate in the long tail with minimal issuance volume, creating a trust surface far larger than the market footprint suggests.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across the four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and only 38 CA owners achieve universal inclusion. Microsoft's store contains 142 roots that Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple do not trust, creating operational complexity where certificate chains validated by Edge fail in other browsers. Store disagreement compounds the concentration risk visible in market share data, as CAs must navigate divergent inclusion criteria while end users expect consistent trust decisions across platforms.
intros.conc: The CR3 concentration of 71% and HHI of 1984 place the WebPKI in a high-risk dependency posture, where operational failure at any of the top three CAs would impact nearly three-quarters of all HTTPS connections. Let's Encrypt alone secures nearly one-third of the encrypted web, creating a single point of systemic failure despite the presence of 88 trusted CAs. This concentration has grown as automation and zero-cost issuance favor scale, leaving the ecosystem structurally dependent on a handful of operators.
intros.tail: 74 CAs operate with minimal issuance volume yet retain full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk where a long-tail CA incident carries the same browser impact as a breach at a top-five provider. These low-volume CAs account for less than 12% of issuance but represent 84% of all trusted CAs, diluting oversight resources across operators with limited operational maturity. The tail concentrates many of the 30 government-operated CAs and operators in high-risk jurisdictions, compounding the governance challenge visible in incident and audit data.
intros.geo: CAs incorporated in the United States issue 93% of all publicly trusted certificates, with 15 US-based CAs dominating the market while 44 European CAs produce just 7% and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs contribute 0.09%. This geographic concentration mirrors market concentration, as the top five global CAs are all US-incorporated entities. The Americas outside the US and the Middle East/Africa regions have CA presence but effectively zero issuance share, underscoring that trust store inclusion does not translate to operational relevance.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trusted roots across the four stores, collectively issuing 0.09% of certificates but representing outsized jurisdiction and operational risk. These CAs appear disproportionately in the long tail and in high-risk jurisdictions flagged for compelled disclosure concerns. Government CAs operate under different incentive structures than commercial providers, with incident history showing patterns of negligent noncompliance and compliance/ops failure that led to 14 of the 16 recorded distrust events.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled disclosure or surveillance mandates: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong, with India and Turkey rated moderate-risk. CAs incorporated in these regions face legal frameworks that may compel certificate issuance, key disclosure, or silent surveillance, creating systemic risk even when per-CA issuance volumes remain low. The jurisdiction risk layer intersects with the 30 government-operated CAs and the 74-CA long tail, where oversight gaps and state control converge.
intros.ops: 1,700 publicly disclosed incidents span 55 CAs, with misissuance (654 incidents) and governance failures (551 incidents) representing the dominant risk categories. CAs self-report only 30% of incidents, while external researchers (18%) and automated tools (15%) contribute more to discovery than root program oversight (4%) or audits (7%). Policy compliance failures appear in 225 incidents and disclosure failures in 157, indicating that process breakdowns extend beyond technical misissuance into governance and transparency obligations.
intros.crypto: Root certificate algorithms and key sizes span legacy RSA-2048 through modern RSA-4096 and ECDSA P-256/P-384, with the transition to post-quantum cryptography creating compliance surface expansion visible in the regulatory obligations data. Active roots include keys issued as early as the 1990s, creating long-lived cryptographic commitments that interact poorly with the 47-day certificate validity floor approaching in 2029. Standards compliance varies across the 88 trusted CAs, with smaller and government-operated CAs slower to adopt modern cryptographic postures.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events across browser and root programs show that 10 resulted from a pattern of repeated issues and 14 cited compliance or operational failures rather than single catastrophic incidents. Negligent noncompliance (7 events) and demonstrated incompetence (3 events) dominate the posture distribution, with willful circumvention appearing in 3 cases and argumentative noncompliance in 2. The median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement is 1,185 days, giving affected CAs over three years to transition customers but also prolonging exposure for relying parties.
intros.policy: Of 43 active TLS-issuing CAs, 3 remain at risk of failing the March 2026 200-day validity limit and 5 face the March 2027 100-day threshold, based on actual replacement behavior rather than stated capability. The BR Readiness gap exists partly because the compliance surface has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations, with 76% classified as mandatory and zero substantive ballots passed since 2022 despite this expansion. CAs must now track requirements across CA/B Forum baseline documents, four root program policies, WebTrust/ETSI criteria, and overlapping IETF/ISO/NIST standards, creating cognitive load that manifests in the 1,700 incidents recorded in operational risk data.
intros.governance: Root program oversight covered just 18% of incidents in 2025 (Chrome), 10% (Mozilla), and 5% (Apple), down from 68% (Chrome) and 78% (Mozilla) in 2019, while Microsoft contributed zero incident coverage in both periods. Chrome has participated in 738 oversight bugs with 115 recent substantive comments, Mozilla in 820 bugs with 48 recent comments, and Apple in 46 bugs with 6 comments, leaving a governance gap that shifts discovery burden to external researchers and automated tools. The declining oversight rate coincides with the 121-fold expansion in regulatory obligations, suggesting root programs cannot scale supervision to match compliance surface growth.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum has 56 member organizations, but only 21 contribute actively while 35 have made zero ballot or discussion contributions. Sectigo leads organizational participation and Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots with 1 endorsement, concentrating policy development among a small group while the silent majority benefits from trust store inclusion without contributing to governance. This participation gap mirrors the long-tail structure in market share, where 74 CAs operate with minimal issuance but full voting rights in the standards body.
intros.audit: Auditors operating under WebTrust and ETSI standards caught 28% of in-scope incidents that later appeared in public bug reports, meaning 72% of operational failures coexist with clean audit opinions issued in the same period. 42 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit letter timing and incident disclosure, 5 letters contain qualified opinions, and only 12 letters use the ETSI EN 319 403 v3.5 standard introduced to improve rigor. Self-reporting rates remain low at 62% (WebTrust) and 69% (ETSI), while auditor concentration (HHI 553) means a handful of firms surveil the majority of the CA ecosystem with detection rates insufficient to prevent the 1,700 incidents recorded across 55 CAs.
